Adullam
uh-DUL-um
proper noun (place)
Hebrew Adullam (H5725), an ancient Canaanite town in the lowland (Shephelah) of Judah; the meaning is uncertain, possibly "refuge" or "justice of the people." Famous for the cave of Adullam, David's stronghold.

📖 Biblical Definition

Adullam was an ancient town in the lowland of Judah, famous for the cave of Adullam, the stronghold to which David fled from Saul, and where the band of his mighty men first gathered to him. After David escaped from the Philistine city of Gath, "David therefore departed thence, and escaped to the cave Adullam: and when his brethren and all his father's house heard it, they went down thither to him. And every one that was in distress, and every one that was in debt, and every one that was discontented, gathered themselves unto him; and he became a captain over them: and there were with him about four hundred men" (1 Sam 22:1-2). The cave of Adullam is one of the great pictures of the Scriptures. To it came not the strong, the prosperous, and the content, but the distressed, the indebted, and the discontented — the desperate and the marginal of Israel, who gathered to the rejected, anointed-but-not-yet-enthroned king. Under David's leadership these outcasts were forged into the mighty men, the famous warriors of his kingdom (2 Sam 23). It was at Adullam that three of these mighty men broke through the Philistine garrison to bring David water from the well of Bethlehem, which he would not drink but poured out to the LORD (2 Sam 23:13-17). Adullam has long been read by the church as a type of Christ and His kingdom: to the rejected king, despised and outside the centers of power, gather the distressed, the debtors, and the discontented — sinners in need, who find in Him a captain and a refuge, and who are transformed under His leadership into a people of valor. As men gathered to David in the cave, so sinners gather to Christ; the King receives the desperate, and makes the outcast His mighty men.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The cave-stronghold in Judah to which David fled from Saul, where the distressed, the indebted, and the discontented gathered to the rejected king and became his mighty men (1 Sam 22:1-2); long read as a type of Christ, to whom needy sinners gather and are transformed.

ADULLAM, proper noun. Hebrew Adullam (H5725); an ancient town in the lowland of Judah; famous for the cave of Adullam.

The stronghold to which David fled from Saul after escaping Gath (1 Sam 22:1).

There gathered to him "every one that was in distress... in debt... discontented" — about 400 men (1 Sam 22:2).

These outcasts were forged into David's mighty men (2 Sam 23); three broke through to bring him water from Bethlehem's well (2 Sam 23:13-17).

Long read as a type of Christ and His kingdom: needy sinners gather to the rejected King and are transformed into men of valor.

📖 Key Scripture

1 Samuel 22:1-2 — "David therefore departed thence, and escaped to the cave Adullam... And every one that was in distress, and every one that was in debt, and every one that was discontented, gathered themselves unto him; and he became a captain over them: and there were with him about four hundred men."

2 Samuel 23:14-16 — "And David was then in an hold, and the garrison of the Philistines was then in Bethlehem... And the three mighty men brake through the host of the Philistines, and drew water out of the well of Bethlehem... and took it, and brought it to David."

Matthew 11:28 — "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest."

Hebrews 2:11 — "For both he that sanctifieth and they who are sanctified are all of one: for which cause he is not ashamed to call them brethren."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Adullam is corrupted only when the cave is read as bare military history rather than as the great picture of the kingdom it has always been to the church, or when the transformation of the outcasts into mighty men under David is overlooked.

expand to see more

Military-history reduction. The cave of Adullam can be read as a mere stage in David's guerrilla campaign against Saul. The Scriptures and the church have always seen more. The detail of who gathered to David — not the strong and content but the distressed, the indebted, the discontented — is theologically pointed. To the rejected, anointed-but-not-yet-crowned king came the desperate and the marginal, and he became their captain. The cave is the gospel in picture: Christ, the rejected King, receives not the self-sufficient but the needy, the burdened, the bankrupt sinner who has nowhere else to go (Matt 11:28). The desperate who gather to Him find a captain and a refuge.

Adullam has no significant postmodern redefinition. The principal point worth recovering is its long-recognized typology of Christ and His kingdom. As the distressed, indebted, and discontented gathered to David at Adullam and were forged into mighty men, so spiritually-bankrupt sinners gather to the rejected King Jesus and are transformed by Him into a holy people. The King is not ashamed to call them brethren (Heb 2:11). What they were when they came — desperate, marginal, in debt — is not what they became under His leadership. Adullam preaches the gospel of the King who receives the needy and makes them mighty.
